title: A map with an uncertain shortcut

picture.description: A walking map and a museum

passage: An old map shows a shortcut through a courtyard to the museum, but a new leaflet does not include it. Ada wants to give visitors reliable directions rather than assume either source is correct. How will she check?

branches.label: Read the courtyard notice
branches.text: Ada finds the courtyard gate closed. Its notice says that the gate opens at eleven on weekdays, and the museum clock shows ten on Tuesday. A longer public path is already open. Ada adds both the opening time and the public path to her directions.

question.prompt: Why is Ada's revised advice more useful than simply calling the shortcut closed?
choices: The notice proves that the museum never opens on Tuesdays.
The shortcut is available later, while another route works now.
The old map shows that every gate opens at ten.
The public path will close when the courtyard opens.

branches.label: Compare the visitor entrance signs
branches.text: Ada follows the old map to a courtyard door marked Deliveries only. A fresh sign directs museum visitors to the entrance beside the public path. Staff explain that this entrance has replaced the former visitor door. Ada draws the new approach on her map.

question.prompt: Which conclusion is best supported by the signs and the staff's explanation?
choices: The courtyard has disappeared since the old map was printed.
The museum no longer accepts any visitors.
Deliveries and visitors must use the same door.
The old route led to an entrance whose purpose has changed.

hint: Use the opening passage and the evidence in your chosen chapter together. Distinguish a temporary time restriction from a changed entrance.

title: Making the sound exhibit welcoming

picture.description: A museum exhibit with music and written information

passage: The class's exhibit includes a recording of local birds. Some visitors want to hear it clearly, while others want a quiet space to read. Leena can test either of two changes.

branches.label: Offer headphones
branches.text: Leena connects headphones so that visitors can choose whether to listen. A visitor who had covered his ears now stays to read the display, while another puts on the headphones to compare two bird calls. Neither visitor asks for the speaker to be turned back on. Leena notes their different choices.

question.prompt: What does this trial most strongly suggest?
choices: All visitors prefer reading to hearing bird calls.
The recording has become unnecessary for the exhibit.
Letting visitors choose how to listen can meet different needs.
Headphones make every visitor interested in the same bird.

branches.label: Add written descriptions
branches.text: Leena places descriptions beside buttons that play each recording quietly. One visitor reads how a call changes from short notes to a long whistle, then presses a button to hear it. Another compares the descriptions without playing any sound. Both complete the bird-matching task.

question.prompt: Why does the second visitor's success matter to Leena's decision?
choices: It shows that useful information can be available without requiring sound.
It proves that nobody will ever use the recording again.
It shows that written descriptions always take less time to read.
It proves that the two visitors heard identical recordings.

hint: Compare what the two visitors do in your branch. Choose a conclusion supported by this trial, not a claim about every possible visitor.

title: The labels that washed away

picture.description: Seed trays with labels blurred by water

passage: Water has blurred the labels on two seed trays. One contains peas and the other contains beans, but neither has sprouted. Tavi needs a dependable way to identify them before the garden exchange.

branches.label: Check the planting photograph
branches.text: A planting-day photograph shows peas beside a star scratched into one tray's rim and beans beside a circle on the other tray. Tavi finds the same marks on the trays now, although their positions on the bench have been swapped. The scratches are still clear. Tavi writes new labels using the marks rather than the trays' positions.

question.prompt: Why are the scratches stronger clues than where the trays now stand?
choices: A tray's position always shows which seeds it holds.
The scratches remain with each tray even when the trays are moved.
The scratches show that both trays contain peas.
Photographs cannot show the positions of objects.

branches.label: Wait and compare the seedlings
branches.text: The organizer says the exchange can be postponed until the plants grow. Tavi keeps the trays separate and asks the gardener to compare their first leaves with labeled pea and bean seedlings. When the leaf shapes become clear, the gardener can identify both trays. Tavi replaces the blurred labels before offering any plants.

question.prompt: What trade-off does Tavi make by choosing this plan?
choices: Finishing sooner matters more than identifying the plants.
Keeping the trays separate makes identification impossible.
Waiting removes the need to label the plants.
The exchange happens later, but the labels can be based on observable evidence.

hint: Identify the evidence that links a name to a tray. Consider what your chosen plan gains and, if it requires waiting, what it gives up.

title: A promise and a change of plan

title: What the note did not say

a reading club where members left brief notes in a shared notebook
a village where announcements had to fit on a very small noticeboard
a busy community center where messages often left out their background

title: Keep the marks or make it new?
